newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia dlr on high as world comes courting.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia dlr on high as world comes courting.

text.p: The Australian dollar stormed to fresh six year highs Monday as a break of key resistance in New York sparked heavy catch-up buying from investors in Asia.

Traders said a week of consolidation at 81 cents had allowed bulls to regroup and they took advantage of holiday conditions on Friday to snatch the US$0.8150 barrier. U.S. funds out of HongKong expanded the breach this morning and were trailed by local and Singapore investors afraid of missing the boat.
"It been a wild day and there's still enormous demand to be met," said one at a local bank. "There were offers above 82, but the pullback was shallow and we should see US$0.8240 soon."
By 5.00 pm (0600 GMT) the dollar was feeling wanted at US$0.8198/03 having finished at US$0. US$0.8160/65 in New York on Friday after surging from US$0.8106/11 late here.

The lunge higher brought the dollar's gains since the rally began in early November to 3-3/4 cents or almost five percent. It had also breached resistance levels not troubled since late 1990, attracting much interest from technical and options traders who have been big buyers from US$0.7940 upwards.
The reason was clear to see on the charts since the currency descended from a US$0.8450 peak in such a hurry back in 1990 that there was little but open terrain between here and there.

The rally was also fuelled by offshore funds in Japan and Europe desperate for a higher return while yields at home were at wafer thin levels. Australian rates looked positively plump in contrast and attracted funds from as far afield as the Japanese salaryman and the Belgian dentist.

This helped it to a fresh four-year closing high on the yen at 93.23/33, up from 92.05/15 late here Friday and a distant 89.60 just a month ago. The currency reached a 33-month high on the mark and briefly made a 44-month high on the Swiss franc.
The broad-based strength was reflected in its trade weighted index which powered to 60.6, a five year high, from 59.9 Friday.

Analysts expected this influx to last as long as Japanese rates remained near record lows, and that seemed likely to be a while yet given last week's sober Tankan business survey from the Bank of Japan and signs of financial strain in the country's banking system.
There was still a risk that official rates would be cut again in Australia, and there was even talk the Reserve Bank could move after its monthly board meeting on Tuesday.
Most analysts thought this unlikely given that the last easing on November 6 had hardly had time to take effect, but economic data were mixed enough to keep the rumours alive.
Today's figures were a case in part.
Retail trade did rise 1.4 percent in October, but that was well short of the 2.0 percent expected and not nearly enough to compensate for the deep 3.7 percent drop seen in September.
Bulls, however, noted the data covered the period before the last rate cut and since then consumer sentiment had rebounded.

Building approvals for October rose a strong 12.8 percent, dwarfing expectations of a 5.0 percent gain. But some analysts picked holes because all the gains were accounted for by the "other" residential sector -- mainly apartments -- while approvals for private houses actually fell 6.4 percent.
September quarter private sector stocks, or inventories, provided a real surprise by rising 2.3 percent when the market had looked for not much more than a 0.5 point gain.

The increase implied stocks would add 0.5 point to GDP growth for the quarter when analysts had expected a 0.4 point detraction. After some speedy spread sheet work, the median estimate from analysts had been revised up to 0.9 percent for Q3 GDP growth from an original 0.55 percent.
Such a performance would still see annual growth slow to 3.4 percent from 4.5 percent in Q2, but that was pretty respectable by international standards. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
